decks.title: Hydrogen — Part 1: Position and the metals that make it
goals: Justify the position of hydrogen by comparing it with group 1 and group 17
Write balanced equations for hydrogen from water, steam, dilute acids and alkalis
Explain why dilute nitric acid and very reactive or unreactive metals are not used

slides.heading: The first element
slides.body_md: Part 1 — hydrogen has one proton and one electron. Where does it belong in the periodic table, and which metals set it free from water, acids and alkalis?

visual.alt: Flow: position, then water and steam, then acids and alkalis

slides.narration: Hydrogen is the simplest and lightest element. In this part we first ask where it should sit in the periodic table. Then we look at the metals that release hydrogen from water, from steam, from dilute acids and from alkalis.

slides.heading: Where does hydrogen sit?
slides.body_md: Hydrogen is placed at the top of **group 1**, but it does not fit there perfectly. It also resembles **group 17**.

slides.narration: In the periodic table, hydrogen is written above the alkali metals. It has one electron in its only shell, just as lithium and sodium have one electron in their outer shells. But it is also one electron short of a full first shell, a little like fluorine and chlorine.

slides.heading: Like the alkali metals

rows: Ion formed by losing the electron
Charge of the ion in a compound with chlorine

visual.alt: Table comparing hydrogen with sodium

slides.narration: Hydrogen resembles the alkali metals in several ways. Its atom has a single outer electron, and it can lose it to form a positive ion. It burns in oxygen to form an oxide, which is water, and it acts as a reducing agent.

slides.heading: Like the halogens

rows: Electrons needed to fill the shell
Ion formed by gaining the electron

visual.alt: Table comparing hydrogen with chlorine

slides.narration: Hydrogen also resembles the halogens. It is one electron short of a complete shell and can gain an electron to form a negative ion in compounds such as sodium hydride. It exists as two atom molecules, it is a non-metal, and it forms covalent compounds.

slides.heading: Hydrogen from water and steam
slides.body_md: The more reactive the metal, the **milder** the condition needed. Follow the activity series downwards.

rows: Violent; the metal darts about; potassium burns with a lilac flame
Steady bubbles; the solution turns milky

visual.alt: Table of the metals that give hydrogen with cold water, hot water and steam

slides.narration: Sodium and potassium react with cold water, and the reaction is violent. Calcium reacts steadily with cold water. Magnesium needs hot water. Aluminium and zinc need steam, and iron needs steam over the red hot metal. The activity series explains this order.

slides.heading: Steam over a heated metal
slides.body_md: Steam from boiling water passes over the **heated metal**. The gas that leaves is **hydrogen**, collected over water.

slides.heading: Equations: water and steam

visual.alt: Table of eight balanced equations for water and steam

slides.narration: Here are balanced equations for water and steam. The last one is different: red hot carbon takes oxygen from steam and gives carbon monoxide and hydrogen. This mixture is called water gas, and we shall meet it again in the manufacture of hydrogen.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: iron and steam
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Balance $\ce{Fe + H2O -> Fe3O4 + H2}$ and say why the arrow is reversible. How many iron atoms react with 20 molecules of steam?

**Step 1.** Iron oxide has 3 Fe and 4 O, so write $3\ce{Fe}$ and $4\ce{H2O}$ (O: 4 = 4).

**Step 2.** Then 8 H on the left need $4\ce{H2}$ on the right: $\ce{3Fe + 4H2O <=> Fe3O4 + 4H2}$.

**Step 3.** Hydrogen can pass back over hot iron oxide and reverse the change, so steam is passed continuously to sweep hydrogen away.

**Step 4.** Ratio 3 Fe : 4 H₂O, so 20 × 3 ÷ 4 = 15 iron atoms.

visual.alt: Iron and steam in a reversible reaction giving iron oxide and hydrogen
visual.caption: Fe 3 = 3; H 8 = 8; O 4 = 4.

slides.narration: Iron oxide has three iron atoms and four oxygen atoms, so we use three iron and four water. The eight hydrogen atoms on the left give four hydrogen molecules. The reaction is reversible, so steam is passed continuously to carry the hydrogen away. Twenty steam molecules need fifteen iron atoms.

slides.heading: Hydrogen from dilute acids
slides.body_md: Metals **above hydrogen** in the activity series displace it from dilute hydrochloric acid and dilute sulphuric acid.

visual.alt: Table of eight balanced equations for metals with dilute acids

slides.narration: Magnesium, aluminium, zinc and iron all sit above hydrogen. Each of them displaces hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid and from dilute sulphuric acid, forming a chloride or a sulphate. Iron forms iron two compounds, not iron three.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: aluminium and hydrochloric acid
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Balance $\ce{Al + HCl -> AlCl3 + H2}$.

**Step 1.** Chlorine: 3 Cl on the right, so $3\ce{HCl}$ — but hydrogen then has 3 atoms, which cannot make whole $\ce{H2}$ molecules.

**Step 2.** Double everything: $2\ce{Al}$, $6\ce{HCl}$, $2\ce{AlCl3}$; hydrogen is $6$, so $3\ce{H2}$.

**Step 3.** Check: Al 2 = 2; Cl 6 = 6; H 6 = 6.

visual.alt: Two aluminium and six hydrochloric acid give two aluminium chloride and three hydrogen
visual.caption: Al 2 = 2; H 6 = 6; Cl 6 = 6.

slides.narration: Aluminium chloride has three chlorine atoms, which suggests three hydrochloric acid. But three hydrogen atoms cannot make whole molecules. So double everything. Two aluminium and six hydrochloric acid give two aluminium chloride and three hydrogen molecules.

slides.heading: Hydrogen from alkalis
slides.body_md: A few metals also react with a hot **concentrated alkali** and give hydrogen. They form a salt in which the metal is part of the negative ion.

visual.alt: Table of three metals with sodium hydroxide, their equations and the salts

slides.narration: Zinc, aluminium and lead also give hydrogen with a hot strong alkali such as sodium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide. The salts formed are sodium zincate, sodium aluminate and sodium plumbite. With potassium hydroxide the potassium salts are formed in the same way.

slides.heading: Which metals and acids are not used?

rows: Far too violent; they react with the water as well
Copper, silver, gold with dilute acid
Below hydrogen, so no hydrogen is formed
Dilute nitric acid with a metal
It is an oxidising agent; it oxidises the hydrogen to water and gives oxides of nitrogen instead
An insoluble coating of lead sulphate stops the reaction

visual.alt: Table of metals and acids that are not used and the reason

slides.narration: Not every metal and acid pair is suitable. Very reactive metals are far too violent. Metals below hydrogen do not react with dilute acids at all. Dilute nitric acid is an oxidising acid, so it oxidises the hydrogen to water instead of releasing it, and gives oxides of nitrogen.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Hydrogen is placed above group 1 but also resembles group 17.
Na, K and Ca react with cold water; Mg with hot water; Al, Zn and Fe with steam; carbon with steam gives water gas.
Mg, Al, Zn and Fe give hydrogen with dilute HCl and H₂SO₄; Zn, Al and Pb give it with NaOH or KOH.
Dilute nitric acid, very reactive metals and metals below hydrogen are not used.

visual.alt: Summary table of four sources of hydrogen with one example each

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Hydrogen is placed above group one, with some features of group seventeen. Metals release it from water, steam, dilute acids and alkalis, and the activity series decides how easily. Dilute nitric acid is never used.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Give the condition with the metal: cold water, hot water or steam.
Iron and steam gives Fe₃O₄, not Fe₂O₃, and the arrow is reversible.
Write the salts from alkalis as zincate, aluminate and plumbite, with the metal in the negative part.
Say that nitric acid is an oxidising agent, not just "it is too strong".

rows: Writing the product of Na and cold water as Na₂O
Saying copper gives hydrogen with dilute acid

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Exam tips. Always give the condition with the metal. Remember that iron and steam give the black oxide and the reaction is reversible. Write zincate, aluminate and plumbite correctly. And explain nitric acid as an oxidising agent.

slides.heading: Making hydrogen in bulk and in the laboratory
slides.body_md: Part 2 — a small amount in the laboratory from **zinc and dilute acid**, and tonnes in industry by the **Bosch process**.

visual.alt: Flow: zinc and dilute acid, or the Bosch process, both give hydrogen

slides.narration: This part covers two methods of making hydrogen. In the laboratory we use zinc and a dilute acid. In industry the Bosch process makes hydrogen from steam and coke on a very large scale.

slides.heading: Choosing the materials

rows: Reacts at a moderate rate; sodium is too violent, magnesium too fast, iron too slow

rows: Hydrogen is almost insoluble in water and is lighter than the water it pushes out
You can see when the jar is full, and the gas is not mixed with air
Why not downward displacement of air
Hydrogen is lighter than air, so it would float upwards and escape

visual.alt: Table explaining collection of hydrogen over water

slides.narration: Hydrogen is collected by downward displacement of water. It is almost insoluble in water, so it pushes the water out of the jar. You can see when the jar is full, and the gas is pure. Hydrogen is lighter than air, so it cannot be collected by displacing air downwards.

slides.body_md: The gas may carry **acid spray**, **traces of other gases** from impure zinc, and **moisture**.

A wash bottle of alkali solution takes out the acid gases, and a drying agent takes out the moisture.

rows: Make sure the joints are airtight
Hydrogen would escape and air could enter
A mixture of hydrogen and air explodes
Reject the first jar of gas

slides.narration: Always keep flames away because hydrogen mixed with air explodes. Check that the joints are airtight. Throw away the first jar, which holds air from the flask. Test a small sample with a flame behind a screen. A quiet pop means the gas is pure, and a loud bang means air is present.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a laboratory preparation
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A student adds dilute sulphuric acid to zinc granules. Write the equation, give two observations and say which gas test is used.

**Step 1.** $\ce{Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2}$ — zinc sulphate dissolves, so nothing coats the zinc.

**Step 2.** Observations: bubbles of a colourless gas; the zinc slowly gets smaller; the flask warms slightly.

**Step 3.** Test: the gas burns with a **pop** when a flame is brought near.

visual.alt: Zinc and dilute sulphuric acid give zinc sulphate and hydrogen
visual.caption: Hydrogen burns with a pop.

slides.narration: Zinc and dilute sulphuric acid give zinc sulphate and hydrogen. Zinc sulphate dissolves, so the zinc stays clean and the reaction continues. You see bubbles of a colourless gas, and the flask becomes slightly warm. The gas burns with a pop near a flame.

slides.heading: The Bosch process: stage one
slides.body_md: Steam is passed over red-hot **coke** at about one thousand degrees Celsius. The product is **water gas**, a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen.

visual.alt: Carbon and steam give carbon monoxide and hydrogen, which is water gas
visual.caption: Water gas: equal numbers of CO and H₂ molecules.

slides.narration: In the first stage of the Bosch process, steam passes over red hot coke. The carbon takes oxygen from the steam. The products are carbon monoxide and hydrogen, which together are called water gas.

slides.heading: Stage two: more hydrogen from the carbon monoxide
slides.body_md: Water gas is mixed with more steam and passed over **iron(III) oxide** with **chromium(III) oxide** at about **450 °C**.

visual.alt: Carbon monoxide and steam give carbon dioxide and more hydrogen
visual.caption: Iron(III) oxide is the catalyst; chromium(III) oxide is the promoter.

slides.narration: In the second stage, water gas is mixed with more steam and passed over iron three oxide, with chromium three oxide as a promoter, at about four hundred and fifty degrees Celsius. The carbon monoxide turns into carbon dioxide and gives still more hydrogen.

slides.heading: Quick check: Bosch conditions
slides.body_md: Match the catalyst and temperature.

visual.alt: Flow: water gas and steam over a catalyst give hydrogen and carbon dioxide

slides.narration: In the second stage of the Bosch process, which substance acts as the catalyst, and what is formed from carbon monoxide?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: counting hydrogen
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** 30 carbon atoms react with steam (stage one), and all the carbon monoxide then reacts in stage two. Count the hydrogen molecules.

**Step 1.** One C gives one CO and one H₂, so water gas has 30 CO and 30 H₂.

**Step 2.** Each CO gives one more H₂ and one CO₂, so 30 more H₂ and 30 CO₂.

**Step 3.** Total H₂ = 30 + 30 = **60**.

visual.alt: Table of the numbers of hydrogen, carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide molecules after each stage

slides.narration: Thirty carbon atoms give thirty carbon monoxide and thirty hydrogen molecules in stage one. In stage two each carbon monoxide gives one more hydrogen and one carbon dioxide. So the total is sixty hydrogen molecules and thirty carbon dioxide molecules.

slides.heading: Removing carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide
slides.body_md: The product is mainly hydrogen with **carbon dioxide** and a little **carbon monoxide**.

nodes.label: Hydrogen + carbon dioxide + a little carbon monoxide
Water under pressure or potassium hydroxide solution removes carbon dioxide
Ammoniacal cuprous chloride removes carbon monoxide

visual.alt: Flow: the gas mixture goes through washing steps that remove carbon dioxide, then carbon monoxide, leaving hydrogen

slides.narration: Carbon dioxide dissolves in water under pressure, so washing with water under pressure removes most of it. Potassium hydroxide solution can also absorb carbon dioxide. The last traces of carbon monoxide are taken out by ammoniacal cuprous chloride. What is left is nearly pure hydrogen.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Laboratory: zinc granules + dilute acid; collected by downward displacement of water.
Impurities are removed with alkali solution and a drying agent; keep flames away and reject the first jar.
Bosch process: C + H₂O → CO + H₂ (red-hot coke); then CO + H₂O → CO₂ + H₂ over Fe₂O₃ and Cr₂O₃ at about 450 °C.
CO₂ is removed by water under pressure or KOH solution; CO by ammoniacal cuprous chloride.

visual.alt: Summary table of the laboratory and industrial methods

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2. In the laboratory, zinc and dilute acid give hydrogen, collected over water. In industry, the Bosch process turns coke and steam into water gas and then into more hydrogen. Carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide are removed by washing.

notes.title: Hydrogen: Position, Sources and Preparation — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Position of hydrogen in the periodic table
sections.body_md:
Hydrogen (atomic number 1) has **one proton and one electron**, in a single shell. It is placed at the top of **group 1**, but it also resembles **group 17**, so its position is a compromise.

| Resemblance with alkali metals (group 1) | Resemblance with halogens (group 17) |
|---|---|
| One electron in the outer shell | One electron short of a full shell (two for hydrogen, eight for chlorine) |
| Loses that electron to form a positive ion, $\ce{H+}$ like $\ce{Na+}$ | Gains an electron to form a negative ion, $\ce{H-}$ in sodium hydride like $\ce{Cl-}$ in sodium chloride |
| Burns in oxygen to form an oxide: $\ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O}$ like $\ce{4Na + O2 -> 2Na2O}$ | Exists as diatomic molecules, $\ce{H2}$ like $\ce{Cl2}$ |
| Acts as a reducing agent | Is a non-metal gas and forms covalent compounds with non-metals, such as $\ce{HCl}$ |

**Differences from the alkali metals:** hydrogen is a gas, not a metal; it has no metallic lustre; it does not form a strongly basic hydroxide; its ion $\ce{H+}$ is a bare proton. **Differences from the halogens:** hydrogen is much less reactive with metals and burns in oxygen, which the halogens do not.

Ionic hydrides: $\ce{2Na + H2 -> 2NaH}$ and $\ce{Ca + H2 -> CaH2}$, in which hydrogen is the negative ion. Covalent compound: $\ce{H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl}$.

key_terms.definition_md: Placed at the top of group 1 because it has one outer electron, with some resemblance to group 17 because it is one electron short of a full shell.
A compound of hydrogen with a metal, in which hydrogen is the negative ion, for example sodium hydride.

sections.heading: 2. Hydrogen from water and steam
sections.body_md:
The more reactive the metal, the milder the condition needed. This is the order of the activity series: K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, (H), Cu.

| Metal | Condition | Equation | What is seen |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sodium | Cold water | $\ce{2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2}$ | Floats, melts to a silvery ball, darts about, hisses; the solution turns red litmus blue |
| Potassium | Cold water | $\ce{2K + 2H2O -> 2KOH + H2}$ | More violent; the hydrogen catches fire with a lilac flame |
| Calcium | Cold water | $\ce{Ca + 2H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + H2}$ | Sinks; steady bubbles; the solution turns milky |
| Magnesium | Hot water | $\ce{Mg + 2H2O -> Mg(OH)2 + H2}$ | Slow bubbles; magnesium burns brightly in steam to give the oxide: $\ce{Mg + H2O -> MgO + H2}$ |
| Aluminium | Steam, heated | $\ce{2Al + 3H2O -> Al2O3 + 3H2}$ | The oxide layer on the metal must be broken down by heating |
| Zinc | Steam, heated | $\ce{Zn + H2O -> ZnO + H2}$ | Zinc oxide: yellow when hot, white when cold |
| Iron | Steam over red-hot iron | $\ce{3Fe + 4H2O <=> Fe3O4 + 4H2}$ | Black triiron tetroxide; **reversible** |

**Iron and steam is reversible:** hydrogen can reduce the iron oxide back to iron, so steam is passed continuously to carry the hydrogen away.

**Carbon and steam:** $\ce{C + H2O -> CO + H2}$ with red-hot coke gives **water gas**, a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen.

**Steam set-up:** boiling water supplies steam, which passes over the heated metal in a hard-glass tube; the hydrogen is collected over water.

key_terms.definition_md: A mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen made by passing steam over red-hot coke.
A reaction that can go in either direction, shown by the sign ⇌; iron and steam is an example.

sections.heading: 3. Hydrogen from dilute acids and alkalis
sections.body_md:
**Dilute acids.** Metals above hydrogen displace it from dilute hydrochloric acid and dilute sulphuric acid.

| Metal | With dilute HCl | With dilute H₂SO₄ |
|---|---|---|
| Magnesium | $\ce{Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2}$ | $\ce{Mg + H2SO4 -> MgSO4 + H2}$ |
| Aluminium | $\ce{2Al + 6HCl -> 2AlCl3 + 3H2}$ | $\ce{2Al + 3H2SO4 -> Al2(SO4)3 + 3H2}$ |
| Zinc | $\ce{Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2}$ | $\ce{Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2}$ |
| Iron | $\ce{Fe + 2HCl -> FeCl2 + H2}$ | $\ce{Fe + H2SO4 -> FeSO4 + H2}$ |

Iron gives iron(II) salts (a pale green solution). Aluminium is slow at first because of its oxide layer.

**Alkalis.** Zinc, aluminium and lead react with a hot concentrated solution of sodium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide and give hydrogen. The metal ends up in the negative ion (zincate, aluminate, plumbite):

- $\ce{Zn + 2NaOH -> Na2ZnO2 + H2}$ (sodium zincate); with potassium hydroxide, $\ce{Zn + 2KOH -> K2ZnO2 + H2}$
- $\ce{2Al + 2NaOH + 2H2O -> 2NaAlO2 + 3H2}$ (sodium aluminate); with potassium hydroxide, $\ce{2Al + 2KOH + 2H2O -> 2KAlO2 + 3H2}$
- $\ce{Pb + 2NaOH -> Na2PbO2 + H2}$ (sodium plumbite); with potassium hydroxide, $\ce{Pb + 2KOH -> K2PbO2 + H2}$

**Metals and acids that are not used**
- **Dilute nitric acid:** it is a strong oxidising agent. It oxidises the hydrogen to water as it forms, and is itself reduced to oxides of nitrogen, so hydrogen is not collected.
- **Very reactive metals (sodium, potassium, calcium):** they react violently, and with the water of the acid, so the reaction is dangerous and cannot be controlled.
- **Unreactive metals (copper, silver, gold):** they lie below hydrogen in the activity series, so they do not displace it from dilute acids.
- **Lead with dilute sulphuric acid:** an insoluble coat of lead sulphate stops the reaction.

key_terms.definition_md: The negative ion of zinc in a salt such as sodium zincate, Na₂ZnO₂, formed when zinc reacts with an alkali.
A substance that oxidises another; concentrated or dilute nitric acid oxidises hydrogen to water.

sections.heading: 4. Laboratory preparation of hydrogen
sections.body_md:
**Reaction:** $\ce{Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2}$ or $\ce{Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2}$ (dilute acid, room temperature).

**Why zinc?** It reacts at a moderate rate: sodium is too violent, magnesium too fast and expensive, iron too slow, and copper does not react. Granules are used because powder reacts too quickly. A few drops of copper(II) sulphate solution make the reaction faster.

**Set-up** (see the diagram): zinc granules in a flask; dilute acid added through a **thistle funnel whose lower end dips below the acid**, so the gas cannot escape up the funnel; a delivery tube leads to a trough of water.

**Collection:** by **downward displacement of water**. Hydrogen is almost insoluble in water, so it pushes the water out of a jar standing upside down in the trough. You can see when the jar is full and the gas is not mixed with air. Hydrogen is lighter than air, so it cannot be collected by downward displacement of air.

**Impurities and their removal:** the gas may carry acid spray, traces of gases from impurities in the zinc (such as hydrogen sulphide) and moisture. It is passed through a wash bottle of alkali solution (for acid gases) and then dried with anhydrous calcium chloride or concentrated sulphuric acid. When the gas is collected over water it is not dry.

**Precautions**
- Make sure all joints are airtight.
- Keep flames away: a mixture of hydrogen and air explodes.
- Reject the first jar of gas, which contains air from the flask; test a sample with a flame — a quiet pop shows the gas is pure.
- Add acid slowly, and use dilute acid; concentrated acid gives other gases.

**Test for hydrogen:** it burns with a pop when a lighted splint is brought near; it is colourless and odourless.

key_terms.definition_md: Collection of a gas that is almost insoluble in water by letting it push the water out of an inverted jar.
A funnel with a long stem used to add liquid to a flask; the lower end must dip below the liquid.

sections.heading: 5. Industrial manufacture: the Bosch process
sections.body_md:
**Stage 1: water gas.** Steam is passed over red-hot coke at about 1000 °C:

$\ce{C + H2O -> CO + H2}$ (water gas: carbon monoxide and hydrogen).

**Stage 2: conversion of carbon monoxide.** Water gas is mixed with more steam and passed over a catalyst of **iron(III) oxide** ($\ce{Fe2O3}$), with **chromium(III) oxide** ($\ce{Cr2O3}$) as a promoter, at about **450 °C**:

$\ce{CO + H2O <=> CO2 + H2}$

**Removal of the gases from the hydrogen**
- **Carbon dioxide** is removed by washing with **water under pressure** (carbon dioxide is more soluble under pressure) or by **potassium hydroxide solution**: $\ce{CO2 + 2KOH -> K2CO3 + H2O}$.
- **Carbon monoxide** (the small amount that is left) is removed by **ammoniacal cuprous chloride** solution.

The product is nearly pure hydrogen. Count of molecules: 30 carbon atoms give 30 CO and 30 H₂ in stage 1, and a further 30 H₂ and 30 CO₂ in stage 2, so 60 H₂ in all.

key_terms.definition_md: Industrial manufacture of hydrogen from water gas and steam over a catalyst, followed by removal of carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide.
A substance that improves the working of a catalyst, such as chromium(III) oxide in the Bosch process.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving sodium oxide, not sodium hydroxide, as the product of sodium and cold water.
- Forgetting the condition: cold water, hot water or steam; or writing a reversible arrow for the wrong metals (it is iron and steam).
- Writing Fe₂O₃ for iron and steam; it is Fe₃O₄.
- Using brackets for zincate, aluminate or plumbite; write the salts as Na₂ZnO₂, NaAlO₂ and Na₂PbO₂.
- Drawing the thistle funnel above the acid level, or collecting by upward displacement of air.
- Saying nitric acid is "too strong" without saying that it is an oxidising agent.
- Mixing up the removal of carbon dioxide (water under pressure or potassium hydroxide) with that of carbon monoxide (ammoniacal cuprous chloride).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a balanced equation, a condition, a name, or one observation.
- 2 marks: an equation with its condition, or a precaution with its reason.
- 3 marks: three equations, or a labelled diagram of the apparatus.
- 10-mark structured question: a situation or set-up with parts of 2 to 4 marks: equations, observations, reasons, a diagram and a count from an equation.

hydrogen is given off and sodium zincate is formed

questions.solution_md: Zinc is one of the metals that react with a strong alkali to give hydrogen and a zincate, option (d).

questions.stem_md: In the preparation of hydrogen the lower end of the thistle funnel must dip below the surface of the acid so that

options.text_md: the gas cannot escape through the funnel
the acid cannot touch the zinc
the gas is dried as it passes up the tube

questions.solution_md: Acid forms a liquid seal at the funnel end, so the hydrogen is forced along the delivery tube, option (a).

questions.stem_md: Hydrogen from the flask is first passed through alkali solution and then over anhydrous calcium chloride. The calcium chloride removes
questions.solution_md: A drying agent takes out moisture; the acid gases were already taken out by the alkali, option (d).

questions.stem_md: In the second stage of the Bosch process the catalyst used, and the substance that carbon monoxide is changed into, are

options.text_md: chromium(III) oxide, with iron(III) oxide as the promoter; carbon dioxide

questions.solution_md: Iron(III) oxide is the catalyst, chromium(III) oxide the promoter, and carbon monoxide with steam gives carbon dioxide, option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which statement shows that hydrogen resembles the halogens?

options.text_md: It gains one electron to form the hydride ion in sodium hydride
It burns in oxygen to give an oxide
It acts as a reducing agent
It has a single electron in its outer shell

questions.solution_md: Gaining an electron to form a negative ion is the halogen-like behaviour; the other three resemble the alkali metals, option (a).

questions.stem_md: The electronic configurations of three atoms are P: 1; Q: 2, 8, 1; R: 2, 8, 7. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: P and R have the same number of outer electrons
Q and R each need one electron to complete the outer shell
P and Q have the same number of outer electrons, and P and R each need one electron to complete the outer shell
P and Q each need one electron to complete the outer shell

questions.solution_md: P and Q each have one outer electron. P needs one to reach two, and R needs one to reach eight; Q needs seven, option (c).

questions.stem_md: Hydrogen burns in oxygen to form water. This is a point of resemblance between hydrogen and

options.text_md: the halogens, which burn readily in oxygen
the alkali metals, which burn in oxygen to form oxides
the noble gases, which burn in oxygen to form oxides
the alkali metals, which form hydrides when they burn in oxygen

questions.solution_md: Water is the oxide of hydrogen, just as sodium oxide is the oxide of sodium, option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Hydrogen is placed at the top of group 1 in the periodic table.

**Reason (R):** A hydrogen atom has one electron in its outer shell, as the atoms of the alkali metals have.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The number of outer electrons is the reason for the group 1 position, so (R) explains (A), option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Hydrogen is a metal because it is placed in group 1.
questions.solution_md: False. Hydrogen is a non-metal gas; its group 1 position is due to its single outer electron.

questions.stem_md: In sodium hydride, hydrogen is present as the negatively charged ___ ion.
questions.solution_md: The negative ion of hydrogen is the **hydride** ion.

questions.stem_md: Write the balanced equation for the burning of hydrogen in oxygen.
questions.solution_md: Two hydrogen molecules combine with one oxygen molecule.

questions.stem_md: State two points of resemblance between hydrogen and the alkali metals.

answer.model_answer_md: Both have **one electron in the outer shell** and both can **lose it to form a positive ion** (also: both burn in oxygen to form an oxide; both are reducing agents).

questions.solution_md: One outer electron; positive ion; oxide on burning; reducing action (any two).

questions.stem_md: State two ways in which hydrogen differs from the alkali metals.

answer.model_answer_md: Hydrogen is a **non-metal gas** with no metallic lustre, while the alkali metals are soft, shiny metals. Hydrogen does not form a strongly basic hydroxide as the alkali metals do.

questions.solution_md: Gas, not a metal; no basic hydroxide.

marking_scheme.step: No strongly basic hydroxide or other valid difference

questions.stem_md: Hydrogen can lose its electron or gain one. (a) Name the ion formed when a hydrogen atom loses its electron. (b) Name the ion formed when it gains an electron. (c) Write the formula of one compound that contains the ion named in (b).

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The **hydrogen ion** (a proton), H⁺.

**(b)** The **hydride ion**, H⁻.

**(c)** **Sodium hydride, NaH** (or calcium hydride, CaH₂).

questions.solution_md: Hydrogen ion; hydride ion; NaH or CaH₂.

questions.stem_md: Small pieces of calcium are dropped into cold water. Which observation is correct?

options.text_md: The calcium floats and melts into a silvery ball
The calcium sinks, steady bubbles of gas form and the water turns milky
The calcium burns on the surface with a lilac flame
Nothing happens until the water is heated

questions.solution_md: Calcium is denser than water and reacts steadily; calcium hydroxide, which is sparingly soluble, turns the water milky, option (b).

questions.stem_md: Of the metals sodium, calcium, magnesium and iron, the one that needs steam passed over the red-hot metal to give hydrogen is
questions.solution_md: Iron is the least reactive of the four, so it needs the most severe condition, option (d).

questions.stem_md: Steam is passed over strongly heated zinc. The gas formed and the solid left are

options.text_md: oxygen and zinc oxide, which is yellow when hot
hydrogen and zinc oxide, which is yellow when hot
hydrogen and zinc hydroxide, which is white

questions.solution_md: Zinc takes oxygen from steam to give zinc oxide and hydrogen; zinc oxide is yellow when hot, option (b).

questions.stem_md: The mixture of gases obtained by passing steam over red-hot coke is called water gas. It contains
questions.solution_md: Carbon takes one oxygen atom from steam, giving carbon monoxide and hydrogen, option (c).

questions.stem_md: A metal M gives no hydrogen with cold or hot water but gives hydrogen when steam is passed over it while it is strongly heated. M could be
questions.solution_md: Sodium and calcium react with cold water and magnesium with hot water, so only zinc fits, option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which equation correctly represents the reaction of potassium with cold water?
questions.solution_md: Only option (a) has equal numbers of K, O and H on both sides, and potassium gives KOH, not K(OH)₂.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Magnesium reacts with hot water but not appreciably with cold water.

**Reason (R):** Magnesium is more reactive than sodium.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Magnesium needs hot water, which is true; but sodium is more reactive than magnesium, so (R) is false, option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Magnesium reacts vigorously with cold water and gives hydrogen.
questions.solution_md: False. Magnesium reacts only slowly with hot water; with steam it burns brightly.

questions.stem_md: The reaction of iron with steam is ___ and the oxide formed is ___ .
questions.solution_md: The reaction is **reversible** and the oxide is **triiron tetroxide**, Fe₃O₄.

questions.stem_md: Write the balanced equation for the action of steam on heated aluminium.
questions.solution_md: Two aluminium atoms need three oxygen atoms for one Al₂O₃.

questions.stem_md: Write the balanced equation for the reaction of calcium with cold water.

answer.model_answer_md: $\ce{Ca + 2H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + H2}$

questions.solution_md: Calcium hydroxide needs two hydroxide groups, so two water molecules.

questions.stem_md: Steam reacts with excess red-hot iron: $\ce{3Fe + 4H2O <=> Fe3O4 + 4H2}$. How many atoms of iron are used up when 20 molecules of steam react?
questions.solution_md: Three iron atoms react with four steam molecules, so 20 × 3 ÷ 4 = 15 atoms.

questions.stem_md: A small piece of sodium is dropped into a trough of cold water. State two observations.

answer.model_answer_md: The sodium **floats** and **melts into a silvery ball**, which **darts about on the water with a hissing sound**. (Any two; the solution also turns red litmus blue.)

questions.solution_md: Floats, melts to a ball, darts about, hisses.

questions.stem_md: Explain why the action of steam on red-hot iron is said to be reversible, and why steam is passed continuously.

answer.model_answer_md: Hydrogen formed can **reduce the iron oxide back to iron** and steam, so the reaction can go both ways. Passing steam continuously **sweeps the hydrogen away**, so the change goes forward.

questions.solution_md: Hydrogen reduces the oxide back; a steady flow of steam removes the hydrogen.

marking_scheme.step: Hydrogen removed by the flow of steam

questions.stem_md: Write balanced equations for the action of (a) hot water on magnesium, (b) steam on heated zinc, (c) steam on red-hot carbon.
questions.solution_md: Mg(OH)₂ with H₂; ZnO with H₂; CO with H₂.

questions.stem_md: Which pair of substances does not produce hydrogen?
questions.solution_md: Copper lies below hydrogen in the activity series and cannot displace it, option (a).

questions.stem_md: Aluminium foil is warmed with concentrated sodium hydroxide solution. The gas given off and the salt formed are
questions.solution_md: Aluminium gives hydrogen and the salt sodium aluminate, with the metal in the negative ion, option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which equation correctly describes the reaction of iron with dilute hydrochloric acid?
questions.solution_md: Iron forms iron(II) chloride and hydrogen is released as molecules, option (c).

questions.stem_md: Iron nails are dropped into dilute nitric acid, but no hydrogen can be collected. This is because nitric acid

options.text_md: is too weak an acid to displace hydrogen from iron
raises iron above hydrogen in the activity series
oxidises the hydrogen to water and is itself reduced to oxides of nitrogen
dissolves the hydrogen as soon as it forms

questions.solution_md: Nitric acid is an oxidising agent, so the hydrogen does not escape, option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which metal gives hydrogen with dilute hydrochloric acid and also with hot concentrated sodium hydroxide solution?
questions.solution_md: Magnesium and iron do not react with the alkali, and copper does not react with either; zinc does with both, option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Zinc gives hydrogen when it is dropped into dilute nitric acid.

**Reason (R):** Dilute nitric acid is an oxidising agent.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Because nitric acid is an oxidising agent the hydrogen is oxidised to water, so (A) is false and (R) is true, option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Zinc reacts with potassium hydroxide solution to give potassium zincate and hydrogen.
questions.solution_md: True: Zn + 2KOH → K₂ZnO₂ + H₂.

questions.stem_md: Write the balanced equation for the action of hot concentrated potassium hydroxide solution on lead.

answer.model_answer_md: $\ce{Pb + 2KOH -> K2PbO2 + H2}$

questions.solution_md: Lead gives potassium plumbite and hydrogen.

questions.stem_md: Name the salt formed when zinc reacts with sodium hydroxide solution.

answer.model_answer_md: **Sodium zincate.**

questions.solution_md: The zinc is in the negative ion, so the salt is sodium zincate.

questions.stem_md: Write the balanced equation for magnesium with dilute sulphuric acid.

answer.model_answer_md: $\ce{Mg + H2SO4 -> MgSO4 + H2}$

questions.solution_md: Magnesium sulphate and hydrogen.

questions.stem_md: Excess aluminium is added to dilute hydrochloric acid: $\ce{2Al + 6HCl -> 2AlCl3 + 3H2}$. How many molecules of hydrogen are formed from 18 molecules of hydrogen chloride?
questions.solution_md: Six HCl give three H₂, so 18 × 3 ÷ 6 = 9 molecules.

questions.stem_md: Aluminium reacts with sodium hydroxide solution: $\ce{2Al + 2NaOH + 2H2O -> 2NaAlO2 + 3H2}$. How many molecules of hydrogen are formed from 12 atoms of aluminium?
questions.solution_md: Two Al give three H₂, so 12 × 3 ÷ 2 = 18 molecules.

questions.stem_md: Iron filings are added to dilute hydrochloric acid. Name the two products and state one observation.

answer.model_answer_md: **Iron(II) chloride** and **hydrogen** are formed. Bubbles of a colourless gas appear and the solution slowly turns **pale green**.

questions.solution_md: Iron(II) chloride and hydrogen; bubbles or a pale green solution.

questions.stem_md: Explain why copper does not give hydrogen when it is added to dilute hydrochloric acid.

answer.model_answer_md: Copper is **below hydrogen in the activity series**, so it is less reactive than hydrogen and **cannot displace it** from the acid.

questions.solution_md: Copper lies below hydrogen in the series and cannot displace it.

questions.stem_md: Give one reason each why hydrogen is not prepared in the laboratory from (a) sodium and dilute hydrochloric acid, (b) silver and dilute hydrochloric acid, (c) zinc and dilute nitric acid.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The reaction is **violent and dangerous** (sodium also reacts with the water).

**(b)** Silver is **below hydrogen**, so there is **no reaction**.

**(c)** Nitric acid is an **oxidising agent**; it oxidises the hydrogen to water and gives oxides of nitrogen.

questions.solution_md: Violent; no displacement; oxidising agent.

questions.stem_md: Granulated zinc, and not zinc powder, is used to prepare hydrogen in the laboratory because granules

options.text_md: do not react with dilute acids
give a larger volume of hydrogen for the same mass
become coated with zinc sulphate that stops the reaction
react at a moderate, controllable rate

questions.solution_md: Powder has a large surface and reacts too quickly; granules give a steady stream, option (d).

questions.stem_md: Hydrogen can be collected over water because it is

options.text_md: slightly soluble and forms an acid with water
a gas that dissolves to give an alkaline solution

questions.solution_md: Only a gas that hardly dissolves can be collected over water; being lighter than air is a different property, option (a).

questions.stem_md: A student lights the first test tube of gas collected in the preparation of hydrogen, and it burns with a loud explosion. The most likely reason is that

options.text_md: the tube contained a mixture of hydrogen and the air that was in the flask
zinc sulphate had formed in the tube

questions.solution_md: Hydrogen mixed with air explodes; the air in the flask is expelled first, option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is not a precaution in the laboratory preparation of hydrogen?

options.text_md: Making sure all the joints are airtight
Keeping all flames away from the apparatus
Making the lower end of the thistle funnel dip below the acid
Heating the flask strongly to speed up the reaction

questions.solution_md: Zinc and dilute acid react well at room temperature; strong heating is not needed and is unsafe, option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Hydrogen collected over water from zinc and dilute acid is completely dry.
questions.solution_md: False. The gas is in contact with water in the jar, so it is moist.

questions.stem_md: In the laboratory, hydrogen is collected by the downward ___ of ___ .
questions.solution_md: By the downward **displacement** of **water**.

questions.stem_md: Write the balanced equation for the preparation of hydrogen from zinc and dilute hydrochloric acid.

answer.model_answer_md: $\ce{Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2}$

questions.solution_md: Zinc chloride and hydrogen.

questions.stem_md: Name one substance used to dry hydrogen.

answer.model_answer_md: **Anhydrous calcium chloride** (or concentrated sulphuric acid).

questions.solution_md: Any drying agent that does not react with hydrogen.

questions.stem_md: Why is zinc chosen in preference to magnesium and to iron for the laboratory preparation of hydrogen?

answer.model_answer_md: **Magnesium reacts too fast** to control, and **iron reacts too slowly**; zinc reacts at a **moderate, steady rate**.

questions.solution_md: Magnesium too fast, iron too slow, zinc moderate.

marking_scheme.step: Magnesium too fast and iron too slow

questions.stem_md: State two precautions to be taken when hydrogen is prepared in the laboratory, with a reason for each.

answer.model_answer_md: Keep **flames away**, because hydrogen mixed with air explodes. Reject the **first jar of gas**, because it contains air from the flask. (Also: airtight joints so that gas does not leak.)

questions.solution_md: Flames away because of explosion; first jar rejected because of air.

questions.stem_md: In the preparation of hydrogen, give a reason for (a) the lower end of the thistle funnel dipping below the acid, (b) using dilute and not concentrated acid, (c) adding a few drops of copper(II) sulphate solution to pure zinc.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The acid seals the funnel, so the **gas cannot escape** through it.

**(b)** Concentrated acid gives **other gases** and the reaction is hard to control (dilute acid gives a steady stream of hydrogen).

**(c)** Zinc becomes coated with copper, which **makes the reaction faster**.

questions.solution_md: Liquid seal; other gases from concentrated acid; copper speeds the reaction.

questions.stem_md: In the Bosch process water gas is mixed with steam and passed over a catalyst at a temperature of about
questions.solution_md: The catalyst chamber is kept at about 450 °C, option (b).

questions.stem_md: The gas mixture that leaves the catalyst chamber of the Bosch process mainly contains

options.text_md: carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide, with a little hydrogen
hydrogen and carbon dioxide, with a little carbon monoxide

questions.solution_md: Carbon monoxide has been changed to carbon dioxide and extra hydrogen; a little remains unchanged, option (d).

questions.stem_md: In the Bosch process ammoniacal cuprous chloride solution is used to remove
questions.solution_md: The last traces of carbon monoxide are absorbed by this solution, option (c).

questions.stem_md: Potassium hydroxide solution can be used to purify the gas from the catalyst chamber because it

options.text_md: absorbs carbon monoxide and forms potassium carbonate
absorbs hydrogen and forms a hydride
absorbs carbon dioxide and forms potassium carbonate
reacts with steam to form potassium carbonate

questions.solution_md: Carbon dioxide is an acidic oxide, so it reacts with the alkali: CO₂ + 2KOH → K₂CO₃ + H₂O, option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The second stage of the Bosch process gives more hydrogen.

**Reason (R):** Carbon dioxide is more soluble in water at high pressure.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Carbon monoxide reacts with steam to give extra hydrogen, so (A) is true. (R) is also true, but it describes the removal of carbon dioxide and does not explain (A), option (d).

questions.stem_md: In the Bosch process chromium(III) oxide is added to iron(III) oxide as a ___ .
questions.solution_md: Chromium(III) oxide acts as a **promoter**.

questions.stem_md: Write the balanced equation for the reaction of carbon monoxide with steam in the second stage of the Bosch process.

answer.model_answer_md: $\ce{CO + H2O <=> CO2 + H2}$

questions.solution_md: Carbon dioxide and more hydrogen.

questions.stem_md: Write the balanced equation for the absorption of carbon dioxide by potassium hydroxide solution.

answer.model_answer_md: $\ce{CO2 + 2KOH -> K2CO3 + H2O}$

questions.solution_md: Potassium carbonate and water.

questions.stem_md: In a plant, 45 carbon atoms in coke react with steam to give water gas, and all the carbon monoxide then reacts with more steam over the catalyst. How many molecules of hydrogen are present in the final gas, before purification?
questions.solution_md: 45 C give 45 CO and 45 H₂; the 45 CO give 45 more H₂, so 45 + 45 = 90 molecules.

questions.stem_md: Name the catalyst and the promoter used in the second stage of the Bosch process, and state the temperature.

answer.model_answer_md: The catalyst is **iron(III) oxide** and the promoter is **chromium(III) oxide**, at about **450 °C**.

questions.solution_md: Iron(III) oxide catalyst; chromium(III) oxide promoter; about 450 °C.

questions.stem_md: Carbon dioxide is washed out of the gas mixture with water under pressure and not at ordinary pressure. Give the reason.

answer.model_answer_md: A gas **dissolves more at high pressure**, so **more carbon dioxide is removed** by the same water.

questions.solution_md: Solubility rises with pressure, so more is dissolved.

questions.stem_md: Water gas is mixed with steam and passed over a heated catalyst. (a) Write the equation for the main reaction. (b) Name the catalyst. (c) State why this step is carried out.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $\ce{CO + H2O <=> CO2 + H2}$

**(b)** **Iron(III) oxide** (with chromium(III) oxide as promoter).

**(c)** It changes the carbon monoxide of the water gas into carbon dioxide and gives **additional hydrogen**.

questions.solution_md: CO + H₂O ⇌ CO₂ + H₂; iron(III) oxide; extra hydrogen.

questions.stem_md: Match each reaction in Column A with the product in Column B that contains the metal.
questions.solution_md: The three alkali reactions give zincate, aluminate and plumbite; steam gives the oxide Fe₃O₄; the acid gives a chloride.

questions.stem_md:
The diagram shows the apparatus used to pass steam over a heated metal. Its parts are lettered A to E.

(a) Name the parts A, C and D. [3]

(b) Name the gas collected in E and describe a test for it. [2]

(c) Zinc is the metal at C. Write the balanced equation and state the colour of the residue when hot. [3]

(d) Why should the delivery tube be lifted out of the water before the burner under C is removed? [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **A** is **boiling water** (in a flask); **C** is the **heated metal**; **D** is the **burner**.

**(b)** **Hydrogen**; it **burns with a pop** when a flame is brought near the jar.

**(c)** $\ce{Zn + H2O -> ZnO + H2}$; the zinc oxide is **yellow when hot**.

**(d)** When the tube cools, the **gas contracts and the steam condenses**, so water would be **sucked back** into the hot glass tube and crack it.

questions.solution_md: Boiling water, metal, burner; hydrogen with pop test; Zn + H₂O → ZnO + H₂, yellow; suck-back prevented.

questions.stem_md:
Four metals P, Q, R and S are known to be sodium, calcium, magnesium and iron, in some order. P floats and darts about on cold water, melting to a ball. Q sinks in cold water and gives steady bubbles, and the water turns milky. R gives only a few bubbles in hot water but burns brightly in steam. S gives no gas with cold or hot water, but a black solid forms when steam is passed over the red-hot metal.

(a) Identify P, Q, R and S. [2]

(b) Write the balanced equation for the reaction of Q with cold water. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:

answer.model_answer_md:

questions.stem_md:
In a hydrogen plant, 30 carbon atoms of red-hot coke react with steam to give water gas. The water gas is then mixed with more steam and passed over a heated catalyst, where 80 percent of the carbon monoxide reacts.

(a) Write the equation for the first stage and name the mixture formed. [2]

(b) Write the equation for the catalyst stage and name the catalyst and the temperature. [3]

(c) Calculate the number of hydrogen molecules in the gas that leaves the catalyst chamber, and the number of carbon monoxide molecules left. [3]

(d) Give two ways of removing the carbon dioxide formed. [1]

(e) Name the substance used to remove the carbon monoxide that is left. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $\ce{C + H2O -> CO + H2}$; the mixture is **water gas**.

**(b)** $\ce{CO + H2O <=> CO2 + H2}$; the catalyst is **iron(III) oxide** (promoter chromium(III) oxide) at about **450 °C**.

**(c)** Stage 1 gives 30 CO and 30 H₂. In stage 2, 80% of 30 = 24 CO react, giving 24 more H₂. Hydrogen = 30 + 24 = **54** molecules; CO left = 30 − 24 = **6** molecules.

**(d)** Wash with **water under pressure**, or with **potassium hydroxide solution**.

**(e)** **Ammoniacal cuprous chloride.**
